Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement with Statistical Guarantees

Zihe Gao  Zhengling Qi  Yifan Cui    Zhejiang University    George Washington University
Abstract

Recursive self-improvement offers a promising path toward AI agents that improve through experience by refining their own harnesses without retraining their underlying large language models (LLMs). Making this self-improvement process reliable, however, requires more than generating new updates: agents must decide which changes are worth keeping. A greedy gate that accepts updates based solely on higher validation scores can mistake an observed gain for genuine progress and lead to performance degeneration, whereas overly conservative statistical gates may reject beneficial updates and hinder performance improvement. We introduce Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing (TRUST), a framework that adapts an online multiple hypothesis testing procedure to control the rate of false evolution across rounds, with an LLM analyzing historical context to help determine how much evidence is required to update the incumbent. Under interpretable assumptions, we prove that TRUST limits the proportion of accepted updates that result in unacceptable performance loss. We further derive a lower bound on the final performance gain. Across the benchmarks HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with the models DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, TRUST reduces the average ratio of accepted inferior updates from the greedy gate’s 45.59% to 2.78%, while achieving higher final scores than the state-of-the-art statistical gate baselines for recursive self-improvement. These findings demonstrate that TRUST strikes a balance between statistical reliability and performance gain in recursive self-improvement.

1 Introduction

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has attracted growing interest for its potential to enhance agents’ capabilities without retraining their underlying language models (Ren et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). In a self-improvement loop, agents modify their own prompts, memory, tools, and workflows to improve task performance (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). This loop can be organized into three components: a solver that executes tasks, a proposer that generates candidate updates, and a gate that decides whether to accept them (Wang et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026).

Existing work has explored mechanisms for generating better candidate updates, while less attention has been paid to deciding when to accept them. A common acceptance approach is to use a greedy gate, which accepts a candidate whenever its score on a fixed validation set exceeds the incumbent’s (Shawn, 2026). Figure 1 illustrates how early gain under greedy acceptance can be lost in subsequent rounds. Noise from finite samples and overfitting from reusing validation data can both make inferior updates appear beneficial and pass a greedy gate (Dwork et al., 2015; Rogers et al., 2016). Accepting a harmful update can reduce the agent’s current performance. The resulting loss may persist through subsequent rounds, ultimately limiting the gain for self-improvement.

Recent work has begun to focus on the acceptance gate (Wu et al., 2025; Shawn, 2026; Sengupta, 2026). RSEA uses an extra validation set separate from the proposal generation set to select candidate updates (Nguyen et al., 2026). PACE provides a safety guarantee for each candidate update through an e-process test in a single round instead of the entire recursive self-improvement process (Shawn, 2026). However, controlling the probability of any false acceptance across rounds can make statistical gates conservative and hinder beneficial updates (Wu et al., 2025; Sengupta, 2026). A key challenge, therefore, remains: retaining opportunities for useful improvement while controlling acceptance errors across rounds under limited validation resources.

We introduce Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing (TRUST), a general statistical acceptance framework. Motivated by false discovery rate (FDR) control (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995; Xu and Ramdas, 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), we define the false evolution rate (FER) as a safety criterion for recursive self-improvement. FER measures the expected proportion of accepted updates that cause an unacceptable performance loss, thereby quantifying the gate’s false acceptance risk. To control FER, we formulate the sequential acceptance decisions as an online multiple testing problem. We also use an LLM to analyze historical context and help the error budget allocator assign less restrictive testing levels to promising candidates. We further draw on noninferiority testing to improve statistical power by allowing a possible loss tolerance (Blackwelder, 1982; Da Silva et al., 2009; Schumi and Wittes, 2011), and use overlap correction to account for bias from reusing validation samples across rounds (Dwork et al., 2015; Rogers et al., 2016). Figure 2 summarizes how TRUST makes recursive self-improvement trustworthy.

Our contributions. We make the following three main contributions: (a) Our framework builds on online multiple hypothesis testing with interpretable parameters, including the error budget, loss tolerance, and overlap correction strength. It naturally incorporates LLM guidance based on diverse forms of historical context. (b) We establish statistical guarantees under explicit assumptions, including FER control, power consistency for improving candidates, and a lower bound on deployment gain. These results connect hypothesis testing criteria to performance gain in recursive self-improvement. (c) We evaluate TRUST in a closed-loop self-improvement harness across HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash. Averaged across these settings, TRUST achieves the highest final gain of 24.84 pp. Compared with the greedy gate, TRUST reduces the mean FER0 from 45.59% to 2.78% and the mean maximum drawdown from 4.963 pp to 0.047 pp, demonstrating high performance gains with few erroneous acceptances and small drawdowns.

2 Related Work

Recursive self-improvement and agent harness.

An agent harness includes tools, context management, and execution control (Shi et al., 2026). Recursive self-improvement agents use feedback to improve various harness components. Promptbreeder evolves task prompts (Fernando et al., 2024). Reflexion, ExpeL, and Voyager convert experience into reflections, insights, and reusable skills, respectively (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). CoEvo-Mem improves memory retrieval (Ye et al., 2026). AFlow and Flow refine agentic workflows (Zhang et al., 2025a; Niu et al., 2025). AgentSquare defines a modular design space with planning, reasoning, tool use, and memory components (Shang et al., 2025). These works focus on proposing effective candidates, while we study whether a new candidate should be accepted to make recursive self-improvement trustworthy. Additionally, we design a harness with diverse editable components in our experiments to evaluate how different gates affect performance and risk.

Hypothesis testing methods.

Multiple hypothesis testing procedures are primarily based on two error criteria: the familywise error rate (FWER) and the FDR (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995; Wang and Ramdas, 2022; Robertson et al., 2023). FWER control is generally more conservative than FDR control. Many popular online FDR methods with p-values rely on independence across tests (Ramdas et al., 2018; Robertson et al., 2023). This independence can be difficult to satisfy when agents evolve based on past feedback. The e-value is an alternative test statistic with a betting interpretation (Shafer, 2021). The e-BH and e-LOND procedures allow arbitrary dependence among valid e-values while controlling FDR (Wang and Ramdas, 2022; Xu and Ramdas, 2024). Drawing on e-GAI (Zhang et al., 2025b) and contextual online testing (Chen and Kasiviswanathan, 2020), TRUST constructs an e-value and allocates the testing levels with context. In RSI, SGM uses statistical tests to decide updates to control FWER across rounds (Wu et al., 2025), while PACE uses an e-process to control the probability of false acceptance in a single round (Shawn, 2026). TRUST provides FER control across rounds and achieves higher final scores than these statistical baselines in our experiments.

3 Problem Formulation

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} denote the distribution of tasks and let u⁡(x,s)∈[0,1]u(x,s)\in[0,1] denote the score of output ss on task xx. For a solver θ\theta, let Sθ​(x,Ω)S_{\theta}(x,\Omega) denote the solver output on task xx under execution randomness Ω\Omega. Define the population score of θ\theta as

J⁡(θ)=𝔼X∼𝒟,Ω​[u⁡(X,Sθ​(X,Ω))].J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mathcal{D},\Omega}\left[u\bigl(X,S_{\theta}(X,\Omega)\bigr)\right]. (1)

We consider a self-improvement process that starts with an initial incumbent solver Θ0\Theta_{0} and initial information ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0}. It recursively generates and evaluates candidates over TT rounds. In round tt, let Q(⋅∣ℱt−1)Q(\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}) denote the conditional distribution of the candidate given the completed history ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} from the fixed proposer. The proposer generates Θ~t∼Q(⋅∣ℱt−1)\widetilde{\Theta}_{t}\sim Q\!\left(\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right), which is evaluated by the gate 𝒢\mathcal{G} against the previous incumbent Θt−1\Theta_{t-1}. Then the gate 𝒢\mathcal{G} produces At∈{0,1}A_{t}\in\{0,1\} and updates the incumbent according to

Θt={Θ~t,At=1,Θt−1,At=0.\Theta_{t}=\begin{cases}\widetilde{\Theta}_{t},&A_{t}=1,\\ \Theta_{t-1},&A_{t}=0.\end{cases}

Different gates may induce different acceptance decisions, thereby changing the subsequent self-improvement trajectories and the candidates proposed in later rounds. These changes can affect the final gain, which is defined as

G⁡(T)=𝔼⁡[J⁡(ΘT)−J⁡(Θ0)].G(T)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[J(\Theta_{T})-J(\Theta_{0})\right]. (2)

We next define the core safety criterion. The population score difference between the selected candidate and the incumbent is Δt=J⁡(Θ~t)−J⁡(Θt−1).\Delta_{t}=J\!\left(\widetilde{\Theta}_{t}\right)-J\!\left(\Theta_{t-1}\right). For a given tolerance level ε∈[0,1)\varepsilon\in[0,1), let Ntε=𝟏{Δt≤−ε}N_{t}^{\varepsilon}=\mathbf{1}\{\Delta_{t}\leq-\varepsilon\}, RT=∑t≤TAtR_{T}=\sum_{t\leq T}A_{t}, and FTε=∑t≤TNtε​AtF_{T}^{\varepsilon}=\sum_{t\leq T}N_{t}^{\varepsilon}A_{t}. Define the false evolution rate (FER) at tolerance ε\varepsilon as

FERε⁡(T)=𝔼⁡[FTεRT∨1].\operatorname{FER}_{\varepsilon}(T)=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{F_{T}^{\varepsilon}}{R_{T}\vee 1}\right]. (3)

Here, FER is the expected proportion of unacceptably inferior updates among accepted updates, and ε\varepsilon specifies the tolerated loss. For ε>0\varepsilon>0, the difference Δt\Delta_{t} is divided into three regions: updates with Δt≤−ε\Delta_{t}\leq-\varepsilon are unacceptable, those with −ε<Δt≤0-\varepsilon<\Delta_{t}\leq 0 are tolerated but not improving, and those with Δt>0\Delta_{t}>0 are improving. Our goal is to ensure that FERε⁡(T)≤q\operatorname{FER}_{\varepsilon}(T)\leq q for a prespecified FER budget qq, thereby providing a statistical safety guarantee for the entire self-improvement process. This helps avoid unacceptable updates, retain beneficial proposals, and may achieve a favorable final gain.

Let 𝒱N=(Z1,…,ZN)∼𝒟N\mathcal{V}_{N}=(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{N})\sim\mathcal{D}^{N} be a fixed validation pool of size NN. Candidate generation uses information from the completed history. In round tt, the sampling plan is to draw n≤Nn\leq N tasks uniformly without replacement from 𝒱N\mathcal{V}_{N} to evaluate the current candidate. All sampled tasks are then returned to 𝒱N\mathcal{V}_{N} so that the next round starts with the full validation pool. Let Kt,iK_{t,i} denote the pool index selected at the iith validation draw, and let Xt,i=ZKt,iX_{t,i}=Z_{K_{t,i}} be the corresponding task. On task Xt,iX_{t,i}, the candidate and incumbent produce the observed score difference

Dt,i=u⁡(Xt,i,SΘ~t​(Xt,i,Ωt,ic))−u⁡(Xt,i,SΘt−1​(Xt,i,Ωt,i0))∈[−1,1],D_{t,i}={}u\bigl(X_{t,i},S_{\widetilde{\Theta}_{t}}(X_{t,i},\Omega^{c}_{t,i})\bigr)-u\bigl(X_{t,i},S_{\Theta_{t-1}}(X_{t,i},\Omega^{0}_{t,i})\bigr)\in[-1,1], (4)

where Ωt,ic\Omega^{c}_{t,i} and Ωt,i0\Omega^{0}_{t,i} denote the execution randomness of the candidate and incumbent, respectively.

Information flow.

Our framework uses filtrations to describe how information accumulates within and across rounds (Ramdas et al., 2023). For clarity, we briefly explain this information flow. The initial information ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} is independent of the validation pool. Let ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} denote the completed history before round tt. Before validation, ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t} additionally fixes the selected candidate Θ~t\widetilde{\Theta}_{t} and testing level αt\alpha_{t} in Section 4. For i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, let ℋt,i\mathcal{H}_{t,i} augment ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t} with the first ii validation samples and their paired outcomes, with ℋt,0=ℱtpre\mathcal{H}_{t,0}=\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}. After validation, ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} contains the decision AtA_{t} and updated incumbent Θt\Theta_{t}. We illustrate this timeline in Figure 3.

4 Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing

The greedy gate accepts a candidate whenever the empirical score difference exceeds zero, making the acceptance decision sensitive to sampling and execution randomness. We formulate candidate acceptance as a hypothesis testing problem. In round tt, we test

Ht0:Δt≤−ε,Ht1:Δt>−ε.H_{t}^{0}:\Delta_{t}\leq-\varepsilon,\qquad H_{t}^{1}:\Delta_{t}>-\varepsilon. (5)

If the null hypothesis Ht0H_{t}^{0} is rejected, the selected candidate is accepted as the new incumbent. Otherwise, the previous incumbent is retained.

In online FDR control, testing levels are allocated across multiple hypotheses under an overall error budget (Chen and Kasiviswanathan, 2020; Zhang et al., 2025b). TRUST adapts this framework to the sequence of candidate acceptance tests defined in (5), using qq as the total FER budget. In round tt, the testing level αt\alpha_{t} determines the acceptance threshold, while the test statistic Mt,m(β)M_{t,m}^{(\beta)} measures the evidence accumulated from the first mm validation observations. For αt>0\alpha_{t}>0, TRUST accepts the candidate at the first m≤nm\leq n when Mt,m(β)≥1/αtM_{t,m}^{(\beta)}\geq 1/\alpha_{t}, following the standard testing rule for sequential e-value testing (Ramdas et al., 2023). If the threshold is not reached within nn observations, the incumbent is retained. When αt=0\alpha_{t}=0, validation is skipped and the incumbent is retained. We next describe how αt\alpha_{t} is allocated and how Mt,m(β)M_{t,m}^{(\beta)} is constructed.

4.1 Testing Level Allocation with Context

We now describe how TRUST allocates the testing level αt\alpha_{t} in round tt under the total FER budget qq. Let BtB_{t} denote the remaining FER budget before round tt, with B1=q∈(0,1)B_{1}=q\in(0,1), and let ρt∈(0,1)\rho_{t}\in(0,1) denote the spending fraction of the remaining FER budget in round tt.

Adapting the e-LORD allocation rule within the e-GAI framework (Zhang et al., 2025b), we combine the adjusted spending fraction ρt\rho_{t} with the remaining budget and the number of accepted updates to determine the testing level

αt=min⁡{αmax,ρt​Bt​(Rt−1+1)},\alpha_{t}=\min\{\alpha_{\max},\rho_{t}B_{t}(R_{t-1}+1)\}, (6)

where αmax∈(0,1)\alpha_{\max}\in(0,1). The resulting charge ctc_{t} for the FER budget and the remaining budget Bt+1B_{t+1} are

ct=αtRt−1+1,Bt+1=Bt−ct.c_{t}=\frac{\alpha_{t}}{R_{t-1}+1},\qquad B_{t+1}=B_{t}-c_{t}. (7)

The charge satisfies 0≤ct≤ρt​Bt≤Bt0\leq c_{t}\leq\rho_{t}B_{t}\leq B_{t}, keeping the balance nonnegative.

We next describe how to determine ρt\rho_{t}. Building on the contextual error budget allocation in online multiple hypothesis testing (Chen and Kasiviswanathan, 2020), we make use of the context CtC_{t} in round tt and use an LLM to analyze it. This context only contains information available before the current round’s validation, including the candidate update and feedback from previous validation rounds. Following the evaluation structure of G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023), the LLM uses explicit criteria to assess the candidate’s potential benefits and risks. Let Ψ\Psi denote the mapping from context to LLM multipliers, with wt=Ψ⁡(Ct)∈[0,∞)w_{t}=\Psi(C_{t})\in[0,\infty). The default spending fraction is set to ρt0=1/(T−t+1)\rho_{t}^{0}=1/(T-t+1), corresponding to an equal share of the remaining FER budget. The LLM multiplier adjusts the spending fraction within the range [ρmin,ρmax][\rho_{\min},\rho_{\max}]:

ρt=clip⁡(wt​ρt0,ρmin,ρmax),\rho_{t}=\operatorname{clip}(w_{t}\rho_{t}^{0},\rho_{\min},\rho_{\max}), (8)

where 0<ρmin<ρmax<10<\rho_{\min}<\rho_{\max}<1 and clip⁡(x,a,b)=min⁡{b,max⁡{a,x}}\operatorname{clip}(x,a,b)=\min\{b,\max\{a,x\}\}. All allocation quantities are determined before validation and included in the information ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t} in Figure 3.

4.2 E-Value Construction with Overlap Correction

Once the testing level αt\alpha_{t} has been determined, the next step is to construct the test statistic Mt,m(β)M_{t,m}^{(\beta)}. We first correct for bias from reusing validation samples. Based on the sampling procedure in Section 3, we define the following index sets to characterize overlap across validation rounds. Recall that Kt,iK_{t,i} denotes the index of the iith validation sample in round tt. Let ℛt,i−1\mathcal{R}_{t,i-1} denote the set of indices not sampled in the first i−1i-1 draws of round tt, and let ℐt,i−1\mathcal{I}_{t,i-1} denote the cumulative set of indices used in validation across the first t−1t-1 rounds and the first i−1i-1 draws of round tt. For each draw, define

Qt,i=𝟏{Kt,i∈ℐt,i−1},ζt,i=ℙ(Qt,i=1∣ℋt,i−1)=|ℐt,i−1∩ℛt,i−1||ℛt,i−1|.Q_{t,i}=\mathbf{1}\{K_{t,i}\in\mathcal{I}_{t,i-1}\},\qquad\zeta_{t,i}=\mathbb{P}(Q_{t,i}=1\mid\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1})=\frac{|\mathcal{I}_{t,i-1}\cap\mathcal{R}_{t,i-1}|}{|\mathcal{R}_{t,i-1}|}. (9)

Here, Qt,iQ_{t,i} indicates whether the current sample has previously been used in validation, while ζt,i\zeta_{t,i} represents its probability under uniform sampling.

We rescale the score difference in (4) from [−1,1][-1,1] to [0,1][0,1] by setting Yt,i=(1+Dt,i)/2Y_{t,i}=(1+D_{t,i})/2, which allows us to use standard e-value constructions for bounded observations (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2024; Ramdas et al., 2023), and the corresponding null boundary in (5) becomes pε=(1−ε)/2p_{\varepsilon}=(1-\varepsilon)/2. We choose β∈[0,1−pε]\beta\in[0,1-p_{\varepsilon}] as the correction strength for bias from data reuse and weight this strength by the exposure probability ζt,i\zeta_{t,i} to obtain the corrected null boundary ut,i(β)=pε+ζt,i​β.u_{t,i}^{(\beta)}=p_{\varepsilon}+\zeta_{t,i}\beta. The sequential e-value evidence is accumulated by setting Mt,0(β)=1M_{t,0}^{(\beta)}=1 and

Mt,m(β)=∏i=1m[1+ηt,iYt,i−ut,i(β)ut,i(β)],m=1,…,n.M_{t,m}^{(\beta)}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\left[1+\eta_{t,i}\frac{Y_{t,i}-u_{t,i}^{(\beta)}}{u_{t,i}^{(\beta)}}\right],\qquad m=1,\ldots,n. (10)

The betting fraction ηt,i∈[0,1)\eta_{t,i}\in[0,1) is chosen based on the information in ℋt,i−1\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1} before observing Yt,iY_{t,i} and controls how strongly the current observation changes the evidence. It can be selected using standard adaptive betting strategies (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2024; Orabona and Jun, 2024; Shekhar and Ramdas, 2023). The complete procedure is presented in Algorithm 1.

5 Theoretical Analysis

We now establish statistical guarantees of our framework, including the validity of the e-value, FER control, power consistency to accept improvements, and a lower bound on the final gain.

Assumption 1.

For any t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T and i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, suppose

𝔼[Yt,i∣ℋt,i−1,Qt,i=1]≤pε+β,if Ht0 is true and ζt,i>0.\mathbb{E}[Y_{t,i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1},Q_{t,i}=1]\leq p_{\varepsilon}+\beta,\quad\text{if }H_{t}^{0}\text{ is true and }\zeta_{t,i}>0. (11)

Reusing validation feedback to construct or select later candidates can lead to optimistic bias in their estimated performance, which is widely studied in adaptive data analysis (Dwork et al., 2015; Rogers et al., 2016). We use β\beta to represent the strength of the correction for data reuse. Assumption 1 connects this correction to our testing by bounding the conditional mean in the e-value construction. We discuss the relationship between β\beta and our algorithm in detail in Appendix A.1.

TRUST may accept the candidate early when the testing threshold is reached and the number of observations is a random variable determined by the observed evidence rather than a fixed number. We formalize this as a stopping time (Durrett, 2019). A random variable τt∈{1,…,n}\tau_{t}\in\{1,\ldots,n\} is a stopping time with respect to the filtration (ℋt,i)i=0n(\mathcal{H}_{t,i})_{i=0}^{n} if {τt≤i}∈ℋt,i\{\tau_{t}\leq i\}\in\mathcal{H}_{t,i} for every i=0,…,ni=0,\ldots,n. We then establish the following conditional validity result.

Theorem 1.

Fix any round t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}. Under Assumption 1, for any m=1,…,nm=1,\ldots,n, the statistic Mt,m(β)M^{(\beta)}_{t,m} defined in (10) satisfies

𝔼⁡[Mt,m(β)∣ℱtpre]≤1,if ​Ht0​ is true.\mathbb{E}[M^{(\beta)}_{t,m}\mid\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}]\leq 1,\quad\text{if }H_{t}^{0}\text{ is true}. (12)

This inequality also holds with mm replaced by any stopping time τt≤n\tau_{t}\leq n with respect to (ℋt,m)m=0n(\mathcal{H}_{t,m})_{m=0}^{n}.

Theorem 1 shows that our test statistic satisfies the conditional validity requirement for e-values described in the statistical literature (Vovk and Wang, 2021; Ramdas et al., 2023). More importantly, validity at arbitrary stopping times τt≤n\tau_{t}\leq n justifies the acceptance rule in Algorithm 1, which stops at τt=min⁡{n,min⁡{i∈{1,…,n}:Mt,i(β)≥1/αt}}\tau_{t}=\min\bigl\{n,\min\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:M^{(\beta)}_{t,i}\geq 1/\alpha_{t}\}\bigr\}. The conditional validity also extends to mixtures of evidence processes using different betting fractions. See Corollary 1 in the appendix. This validity result provides the basis for the following theorem on FER control in RSI.

Theorem 2.

Fix a horizon T≥1T\geq 1 and an FER budget q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1). Under Assumption 1, the false evolution rate of Algorithm 1 satisfies

FERε⁡(T)≤q.\operatorname{FER}_{\varepsilon}(T)\leq q. (13)

Theorem 2 controls the expected proportion of unacceptable updates among all accepted updates over the entire self-improvement process with TT rounds. The same bound in (13) holds with TT replaced by any stopping time τ≤T\tau\leq T with respect to the self-improvement history (ℱt)t=0T(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t=0}^{T}, as established in Appendix C.2. Thus, the process may be stopped based on the observed self-improvement history without losing FER control. In addition, the FER guarantee does not rely on the LLM correctly identifying beneficial candidates. The LLM uses context to allocate more FER budget to promising candidates and less to unpromising ones, safely improving the detection of beneficial updates.

Let It=𝟏{Δt>0}I_{t}=\mathbf{1}\{\Delta_{t}>0\}, UT=∑t≤TItU_{T}=\sum_{t\leq T}I_{t}, and ST=∑t≤TIt​AtS_{T}=\sum_{t\leq T}I_{t}A_{t}. The true evolution rate (TER) is

TER⁡(T)=𝔼⁡[STUT∨1],\operatorname{TER}(T)=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{S_{T}}{U_{T}\vee 1}\right], (14)

the expected proportion of improving candidates that are accepted (Gadbury et al., 2004).

Assumption 2.

Fix TT and ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), and let N,n→∞N,n\to\infty. Suppose that the following conditions are satisfied: (a) There exists a deterministic sequence rN,n→0r_{N,n}\to 0 such that ℙ⁡(UT=0)≤rN,n\mathbb{P}(U_{T}=0)\leq r_{N,n}. (b) n/N→0n/N\to 0. (c) There exist constants η−\eta_{-} and η+\eta_{+} such that, for t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T and i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, the betting fractions satisfy 0<η−≤ηt,i≤η+<2​ε/(1+ε)0<\eta_{-}\leq\eta_{t,i}\leq\eta_{+}<2\varepsilon/(1+\varepsilon).

Assumption 2(a) requires the probability that the proposer fails to generate any improvement to vanish as the sample size grows. As n→∞n\to\infty, the proposer also receives more historical feedback, making it more likely to produce at least one effective improvement. Assumption 2(b) controls overlap by requiring n/N→0n/N\to 0, so the bias caused by overlap becomes very small. Assumption 2(c) can be satisfied in practice by choosing the betting fraction ηt,i\eta_{t,i} within the specified range.

Theorem 3.

Under Assumption 2, there exists a constant κ>0\kappa>0 such that for sufficiently large NN and nn,

TER⁡(T)≥1−rN,n−T​e−κ​n.\operatorname{TER}(T)\geq 1-r_{N,n}-Te^{-\kappa n}. (15)

Hence, TER⁡(T)→1\operatorname{TER}(T)\to 1 as N,n→∞N,n\to\infty.

Theorem 3 provides a lower bound on TER through two terms: rN,nr_{N,n} bounds the probability that no improving candidate is proposed, while T​e−κ​nTe^{-\kappa n} bounds the contribution of gate misses. Both terms vanish as the sample size grows with TT fixed. It also reveals a theoretical role of noninferiority: when ε=0\varepsilon=0, the upper bound 2​ε/(1+ε)2\varepsilon/(1+\varepsilon) in Assumption 2 is zero, then no positive betting fraction satisfies the condition. Under this argument, a positive ε\varepsilon is needed to obtain TER⁡(T)→1\operatorname{TER}(T)\to 1.

We next evaluate the final incumbent through its gain G⁡(T)G(T) defined in (2). Let 𝒫T=∑t=1T𝔼⁡[(Δt)+]\mathcal{P}_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[(\Delta_{t})_{+}] denote the expected total positive effect of the proposed candidates.

Theorem 4.

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, there exists a constant κ>0\kappa>0 such that for sufficiently large NN and nn,

G⁡(T)≥\displaystyle G(T)\geq{} (1−e−κ​n)​𝒫T−∑t=1T𝔼⁡[At​min⁡{(−Δt)+,ε}+αt​(−Δt−ε)+].\displaystyle\bigl(1-e^{-\kappa n}\bigr)\mathcal{P}_{T}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\!\left[A_{t}\min\{(-\Delta_{t})_{+},\varepsilon\}+\alpha_{t}(-\Delta_{t}-\varepsilon)_{+}\right]. (16)

The first term shows that the loss of positive improvement caused by statistical rejection vanishes exponentially with the validation sample size. The second term quantifies the downside from the noninferiority margin. The third term controls loss beyond the tolerance through the allocated testing levels αt\alpha_{t} and may be reduced when the LLM uses historical context to assign smaller testing levels to candidates with greater downside risk. Thus, TRUST asymptotically preserves beneficial updates while keeping harmful acceptance risk under statistical control. Additionally, to measure losses along the trajectory, we define population maximum drawdown (MDD) as MDD⁡(T)=max0≤r<s≤T⁡(J⁡(Θr)−J⁡(Θs))+\operatorname{MDD}(T)=\max_{0\leq r<s\leq T}\bigl(J(\Theta_{r})-J(\Theta_{s})\bigr)_{+}. Appendix E derives an upper bound on expected MDD.

6 Numerical Experiments

We compare the performance gains and acceptance risks of different gates in an editable self-improvement harness, and conduct ablation studies to examine the effects of TRUST’s key parameters. Supplementary diagnostics and case studies in Appendices I and G.4 show that higher validation scores do not necessarily imply better test performance.

Following modular agent design (Shang et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025), our editable harness 𝖧t=(𝖱t,𝖯t,𝖬t,𝖶t)\mathsf{H}_{t}=(\mathsf{R}_{t},\mathsf{P}_{t},\mathsf{M}_{t},\mathsf{W}_{t}) exposes 20 operators across four components: reasoning (Zhou et al., 2023; Fernando et al., 2024), routing (Lewis et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2024), memory (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024), and workflow (Zhang et al., 2025a). Appendix F details operator designs.

6.1 Main gate comparison

Datasets, models and metrics.

We evaluate the benchmarks HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), DROP (Dua et al., 2019), and APPS (Hendrycks et al., 2021) with the models Qwen-3.8-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. For each dataset, the validation sets contain a total of 200 examples, with 300 held-out examples used only as the test set. We use additional 20 examples to construct the initial information ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0}. Test scores are measured by Joint F1 for HotpotQA, official token F1 for DROP, and the test case pass rate for APPS. We report gain and MDD in percentage points (pp). For a stricter empirical diagnostic, we report FER0\mathrm{FER}_{0}, which counts all accepted non-improving updates.

Baselines.

We compare TRUST with four baselines over 30 rounds and 5 seeds. Greedy accepts candidates with higher scores on the validation samples. PACE uses an e-process test to control false acceptance within a single round (Shawn, 2026). SGM-B and SGM-H use Bernstein and Hoeffding tests, respectively, with FWER control across rounds (Wu et al., 2025). For TRUST, we set q=0.30q=0.30, ε=0.10\varepsilon=0.10, and β=0.01\beta=0.01. More implementation details appear in Appendix G.

TRUST achieves high scores in all six settings and the highest scores in four of them (Table 1). It maintains FER0 below 30% in all six settings, whereas Greedy exceeds 30% in every setting. The highest MDD for TRUST is only 0.27 pp, whereas Greedy reaches 8.48 pp. Appendix G.4 presents a case study of Greedy that improves validation performance but harms test performance.

Among the remaining methods with FER0≤30%\mathrm{FER}_{0}\leq 30\%, SGM-B never accepts an update and SGM-H accepts only three updates across all runs, so they show no score improvement in most settings. These results suggest that both methods for FWER control across multiple rounds are conservative in practice. Relative to PACE, TRUST achieves higher scores and TER in all six settings, with FER0 lower in one setting, equal in three, and higher in two.

The left panel of Figure 4 shows the mean gain trajectories over rounds. Greedy achieves rapid initial gains but exhibits subsequent declines. TRUST overtakes Greedy in later rounds and preserves its accumulated gains, achieving the highest final mean gain. The right panel compares mean final gain and mean MDD. We mark the region with mean MDD below 1 pp as an empirical safe area. TRUST lies within this region while achieving the highest among all compared methods, striking a balance between performance gain and stability in RSI.

6.2 Ablation study

We next conduct ablation studies on HotpotQA/DeepSeek-V4-Flash. We vary three key parameters: the FER budget qq, noninferiority margin ε\varepsilon, and overlap correction strength β\beta. We also compare TRUST with and without LLM guidance. Appendix H provides the detailed settings and results.

Figure 5 shows that larger qq and ε\varepsilon make TRUST more aggressive, with higher TER and FER0. Larger β\beta makes it more conservative: FER0 drops from 23.33% at β=0\beta=0 to 0% at β=0.03\beta=0.03. These trends are consistent with the definitions of the three parameters. In each ablation study, the gain first increases, then decreases or holds steady. For β\beta, it peaks at 11.58 pp when β=0.01\beta=0.01, compared with 10.97 pp without correction, suggesting that an appropriate overlap correction strength can be beneficial in practice. Appendix H.1 provides additional trajectory results and a more detailed analysis. These results highlight the importance of balancing conservative and aggressive acceptance to improve performance.

We replace the LLM allocator with the default multiplier wt≡1w_{t}\equiv 1 while keeping other parameters in TRUST unchanged. Figure 6 shows that TRUST achieves a higher final gain, corresponding to final scores of 44.91 ±\pm 1.36% for TRUST and 43.78 ±\pm 1.18% for TRUST without LLM guidance. This suggests a performance benefit from using context to guide the allocation of testing levels. We provide a detailed case study in Appendix H.2 showing how the LLM analyzes context and assigns different LLM multipliers to influence acceptance decisions.

7 Conclusion and Limitations

TRUST applies online multiple hypothesis testing to control FER across rounds in self-improving agents, with LLM guidance and interpretable parameters for adjusting gate behavior. Our theoretical analysis and experiments show that the framework helps balance useful improvement and acceptance error control under limited validation resources. It extends existing statistical methods and provides a flexible statistical foundation for future work on recursive self-improvement. We discuss this point further in Appendix A.2. Overall, we show that TRUST strikes a balance between statistical reliability and performance gains in recursive self-improvement.

The present study does not address how to identify an exact value of overlap correction strength from data or how to optimally tune other parameters. The noninferiority margin provides an interpretable tolerance for loss, but the theoretical guarantee can be conservative and only partly explains practical behavior. The LLM allocator can occasionally make mistakes when judging candidate updates, which may lead to poor choices of LLM multipliers. Optimizing the gate to maximize gain while keeping safety metrics within target ranges is also a promising direction. Future work can address these limitations to make the recursive self-improvement process more trustworthy and effective.

Appendix

Appendix A Supplementary Discussion

A.1 Interpretation of the overlap correction

We do not develop a complete model of validation data reuse in this work. Detailed studies of adaptive data analysis can be found in prior work (Dwork et al., 2015; Rogers et al., 2016; Russo and Zou, 2016; Xu and Raginsky, 2017). Instead, we state sufficient conditions for valid e-values and focus on a framework for FER control across RSI rounds. The interpretation of β\beta is related to how historical validation information, including feedback summarized in CtC_{t}, is used in candidate construction and selection. Greater reliance on information from previously evaluated samples may increase optimism when those samples are reused. For example, later rounds may use a few failed cases from the previous round or summaries of common error types. These forms of feedback reveal different information about the validation data and may lead to different degrees of optimism bias in subsequent evaluation. The parameter β\beta specifies an allowance for this optimism under the null hypothesis. A stronger correction requires stronger validation results to reach the acceptance threshold, making the gate more conservative and potentially limiting both false acceptances and the acceptance of useful updates. Our sensitivity results in Section 6.2 and Appendix H support the practical value of an appropriate correction strength. In the reported ablation, an appropriate β\beta achieves a higher mean final gain than no correction, whereas larger values make the gate overly conservative and reduce final gains.

A.2 Relation to Existing Statistical Methods

TRUST adapts FDR control in multiple hypothesis testing to the acceptance of candidates in self-evolving agents. It provides a framework covering the validation protocol, correction for data reuse, noninferiority testing, construction of test statistics, and allocation of testing levels. Within this framework, an LLM analyzes the candidate and historical context to guide allocation, while statistical guarantees hold under the stated assumptions. Existing statistical studies (Zhang et al., 2025b; Chen and Kasiviswanathan, 2020) compare testing procedures on specified hypotheses and observation streams in their numerical experiments. In our RSI setting, the proposer constructs candidates using historical information. Different gates can produce different acceptance decisions and incumbents, leading to different histories and subsequent candidates. Our experiments follow this closed loop and use update operators motivated by prior work on RSI agents. This allows us to compare how different gates affect both acceptance decisions and subsequent search on real tasks. Our theoretical analysis follows the same adaptive process and connects a lower bound on final gain to the testing levels and other parameters of the gate. It thus provides a statistical foundation for analyzing both acceptance risk and improvement along the trajectory induced by the gate.

Appendix B Proof of Conditional Evidence Validity

B.1 Proof of Theorem 1

In each round, the sampling plan is to draw nn tasks from the fixed validation pool of size NN, where n≤Nn\leq N. All NN sample indices are selectable at the start of the round, so ℛt,0={1,2,…,N}\mathcal{R}_{t,0}=\{1,2,\ldots,N\}. At draw ii, we select Kt,iK_{t,i} uniformly from the remaining set ℛt,i−1\mathcal{R}_{t,i-1} and remove it, giving ℛt,i=ℛt,i−1∖{Kt,i}\mathcal{R}_{t,i}=\mathcal{R}_{t,i-1}\setminus\{K_{t,i}\}. Thus, a sample can be drawn at most once within a round but may be used again in later rounds.

Let Lt,i∈{0,1}L_{t,i}\in\{0,1\} be the ℋt,i−1\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}-measurable indicator that draw ii is made.

Lt,i={1,if draw i is made in round t,0,otherwise.L_{t,i}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if draw $i$ is made in round $t$},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Within each round, sampling proceeds consecutively and does not continue after stopping. If αt=0\alpha_{t}=0, no validation samples are drawn.

Each round uses at most nn samples. The bounds on the betting fractions in Assumption 2(c) apply on draws that are made (Lt,i=1L_{t,i}=1). If sampling stops early, we set the variables for the remaining indices to zero as a notational convention for the proofs:

Yt,i=Qt,i=ζt,i=ηt,i=0when ​Lt,i=0.Y_{t,i}=Q_{t,i}=\zeta_{t,i}=\eta_{t,i}=0\qquad\text{when }L_{t,i}=0.

After stopping, no more samples are used, and the history and record of previously used samples stay unchanged. When a sample is drawn, Qt,iQ_{t,i} equals one with conditional probability ζt,i\zeta_{t,i}. Hence,

𝔼⁡[Qt,i∣ℋt,i−1]=ζt,i.\mathbb{E}[Q_{t,i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}]=\zeta_{t,i}.

After stopping, both Qt,iQ_{t,i} and ζt,i\zeta_{t,i} are set to zero, so this equality still holds.

Lemma 1.

Let (ℋi)i=0n(\mathcal{H}_{i})_{i=0}^{n} be a filtration, Yi∈[0,1]Y_{i}\in[0,1] be ℋi\mathcal{H}_{i}-measurable, and ui∈(0,1]u_{i}\in(0,1] and ηi∈[0,1)\eta_{i}\in[0,1) be ℋi−1\mathcal{H}_{i-1}-measurable for each i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. If

𝔼⁡[Yi∣ℋi−1]≤ui,\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{i-1}]\leq u_{i},

then

M0=1,Mm=∏i=1m[1+ηi​Yi−uiui]M_{0}=1,\qquad M_{m}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\left[1+\eta_{i}\frac{Y_{i}-u_{i}}{u_{i}}\right]

is a nonnegative supermartingale. Moreover, for every stopping time τ≤n\tau\leq n, 𝔼⁡[Mτ∣ℋ0]≤1\mathbb{E}[M_{\tau}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0}]\leq 1.

Proof.

Write Gi=1+ηi​(Yi−ui)/uiG_{i}=1+\eta_{i}(Y_{i}-u_{i})/u_{i}. Since Yi≥0Y_{i}\geq 0, Gi≥1−ηi>0G_{i}\geq 1-\eta_{i}>0. Since uiu_{i} and ηi\eta_{i} are ℋi−1\mathcal{H}_{i-1}-measurable, we have

𝔼⁡[Gi∣ℋi−1]=1+ηiui​(𝔼⁡[Yi∣ℋi−1]−ui)≤1.\mathbb{E}[G_{i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{i-1}]=1+\frac{\eta_{i}}{u_{i}}\left(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{i-1}]-u_{i}\right)\leq 1.

By the product definition, Mi=Mi−1​GiM_{i}=M_{i-1}G_{i} and Mi−1=∏j=1i−1GjM_{i-1}=\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}G_{j}. For j<ij<i, each GjG_{j} is ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j}-measurable, with ℋj⊆ℋi−1\mathcal{H}_{j}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{i-1}. Thus, Mi−1M_{i-1} is ℋi−1\mathcal{H}_{i-1}-measurable and can be taken outside the conditional expectation:

𝔼⁡[Mi∣ℋi−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[M_{i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{i-1}] =𝔼⁡[Mi−1​Gi∣ℋi−1]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[M_{i-1}G_{i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{i-1}]
=Mi−1​𝔼​[Gi∣ℋi−1]\displaystyle=M_{i-1}\mathbb{E}[G_{i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{i-1}]
=Mi−1​[1+ηiui​(𝔼⁡[Yi∣ℋi−1]−ui)]\displaystyle=M_{i-1}\left[1+\frac{\eta_{i}}{u_{i}}\left(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{i-1}]-u_{i}\right)\right]
≤Mi−1.\displaystyle\leq M_{i-1}.

Taking expectations and iterating from M0=1M_{0}=1 gives 𝔼⁡[Mi]≤1\mathbb{E}[M_{i}]\leq 1, so each MiM_{i} is integrable. Together with nonnegativity and ℋi\mathcal{H}_{i}-measurability, this proves the supermartingale claim.

For bounded τ\tau, use the finite pathwise decomposition

Mτ=M0+∑i=1n𝟏{τ≥i}(Mi−Mi−1).M_{\tau}=M_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{\tau\geq i\}(M_{i}-M_{i-1}).

The event {τ≥i}={τ≤i−1}c\{\tau\geq i\}=\{\tau\leq i-1\}^{c} belongs to ℋi−1\mathcal{H}_{i-1}. Hence every stopped increment has nonpositive conditional mean:

𝔼[𝟏{τ≥i}(Mi−Mi−1)|ℋi−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}\{\tau\geq i\}(M_{i}-M_{i-1})\middle|\mathcal{H}_{i-1}\right]
=𝟏{τ≥i}(𝔼[Mi∣ℋi−1]−Mi−1)≤0.\displaystyle\qquad=\mathbf{1}\{\tau\geq i\}\left(\mathbb{E}[M_{i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{i-1}]-M_{i-1}\right)\leq 0.

Since ℋ0⊆ℋi−1\mathcal{H}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{i-1}, the tower property implies that each stopped increment also has nonpositive conditional expectation given ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}. Taking conditional expectations given ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} in the decomposition of MτM_{\tau} above, we obtain

𝔼⁡[Mτ∣ℋ0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[M_{\tau}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0}] =M0+∑i=1n𝔼[𝟏{τ≥i}(Mi−Mi−1)∣ℋ0]\displaystyle=M_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}\{\tau\geq i\}(M_{i}-M_{i-1})\mid\mathcal{H}_{0}\right]
≤M0=1.\displaystyle\leq M_{0}=1.

∎

B.2 Stopping times

Proposition 1.

Suppose αt∈(0,1)\alpha_{t}\in(0,1) is ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable and set

τt=inf{m∈{0,…,n}:Mt,m(β)≥1αt}∧n.\tau_{t}=\inf\left\{m\in\{0,\ldots,n\}:M^{(\beta)}_{t,m}\geq\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\right\}\wedge n.

Then τt\tau_{t} is a stopping time bounded by nn, and

𝟏{Mt,τt(β)≥1/αt}=𝟏{max0≤m≤nMt,m(β)≥1/αt}.\mathbf{1}\{M^{(\beta)}_{t,\tau_{t}}\geq 1/\alpha_{t}\}=\mathbf{1}\left\{\max_{0\leq m\leq n}M^{(\beta)}_{t,m}\geq 1/\alpha_{t}\right\}.
Proof.

For 0≤m<n0\leq m<n,

{τt≤m}=⋃j=0m{Mt,j(β)≥1/αt}∈ℋt,m,\{\tau_{t}\leq m\}=\bigcup_{j=0}^{m}\{M^{(\beta)}_{t,j}\geq 1/\alpha_{t}\}\in\mathcal{H}_{t,m},

because Mt,j(β)M^{(\beta)}_{t,j} is ℋt,j\mathcal{H}_{t,j}-measurable, αt\alpha_{t} is ℋt,0=ℱtpre\mathcal{H}_{t,0}=\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable, and ℋt,0⊆ℋt,j⊆ℋt,m\mathcal{H}_{t,0}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{t,j}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{t,m} for every j≤mj\leq m.

By definition, τt≤n\tau_{t}\leq n for every sample outcome. Therefore, when m≥nm\geq n, we have τt≤n≤m\tau_{t}\leq n\leq m for every outcome, so

{τt≤m}=Ω,\{\tau_{t}\leq m\}=\Omega,

where Ω\Omega is the set of all possible sample outcomes. In particular, {τt≤n}=Ω∈ℋt,n\{\tau_{t}\leq n\}=\Omega\in\mathcal{H}_{t,n}. Together with the case m<nm<n above, this proves that τt\tau_{t} is a stopping time bounded by nn.

If a crossing occurs, the stopped value is the first crossing value; otherwise the process stops at nn below threshold. ∎

B.3 Mixtures

Betting fractions.

Betting interprets an evidence process as capital accumulated from an initial value of one (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2024). In Equation (10), the amount bet on observation ii is ηt,i​Mt,i−1(β)\eta_{t,i}M^{(\beta)}_{t,i-1}, where Mt,i−1(β)M^{(\beta)}_{t,i-1} is the current capital and ηt,i∈[0,1)\eta_{t,i}\in[0,1) specifies the proportion of that capital put at risk. The new capital equals the current capital plus the gain or loss from this bet:

Mt,i(β)\displaystyle M^{(\beta)}_{t,i} =Mt,i−1(β)+ηt,i​Mt,i−1(β)​Yt,i−ut,i(β)ut,i(β)\displaystyle=M^{(\beta)}_{t,i-1}+\eta_{t,i}M^{(\beta)}_{t,i-1}\frac{Y_{t,i}-u_{t,i}^{(\beta)}}{u_{t,i}^{(\beta)}}
=Mt,i−1(β)​[(1−ηt,i)+ηt,i​Yt,iut,i(β)].\displaystyle=M^{(\beta)}_{t,i-1}\left[(1-\eta_{t,i})+\eta_{t,i}\frac{Y_{t,i}}{u_{t,i}^{(\beta)}}\right].

The uncommitted capital is retained, and the amount bet is multiplied by the return factor Yt,i/ut,i(β)Y_{t,i}/u_{t,i}^{(\beta)}. Thus ηt,i=0\eta_{t,i}=0 leaves the evidence unchanged; if Yt,i=0Y_{t,i}=0, the update loses exactly the fraction ηt,i\eta_{t,i} of current capital. Larger betting fractions increase both the gain when Yt,i>ut,i(β)Y_{t,i}>u_{t,i}^{(\beta)} and the loss when Yt,i<ut,i(β)Y_{t,i}<u_{t,i}^{(\beta)}. The amount of each bet is calculated using the current capital. A betting strategy specifies how to choose these fractions from the available history: each ηt,i\eta_{t,i} must be ℋt,i−1\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}-measurable, so it is chosen before observing Yt,iY_{t,i}.

Combining betting strategies.

Let L≥1L\geq 1 be a fixed integer denoting the number of betting strategies included in the mixture. For each ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}, strategy ℓ\ell uses ℋt,i−1\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}-measurable fractions ηt,i(ℓ)∈[0,1)\eta_{t,i}^{(\ell)}\in[0,1) and produces

Mt,0(β,ℓ)=1,Mt,m(β,ℓ)=∏i=1m[1+ηt,i(ℓ)​Yt,i−ut,i(β)ut,i(β)].M_{t,0}^{(\beta,\ell)}=1,\qquad M_{t,m}^{(\beta,\ell)}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\left[1+\eta_{t,i}^{(\ell)}\frac{Y_{t,i}-u_{t,i}^{(\beta)}}{u_{t,i}^{(\beta)}}\right].

All LL processes use the same validation observations and corrected boundaries, with potentially different betting fractions. A mixture combines their evidence by taking a weighted average, allowing several betting strategies to contribute to the test (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2024). The weight πt,ℓ\pi_{t,\ell} is the fraction of initial capital assigned to strategy ℓ\ell; the weights are nonnegative, sum to one, are ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable, and remain fixed throughout the round. Convex averaging preserves e-value validity even when the component e-values depend on the same observations (Vovk and Wang, 2021). The following corollary establishes the corresponding conditional validity for these sequential processes.

Corollary 1.

Let Mt,m(β,1),…,Mt,m(β,L)M_{t,m}^{(\beta,1)},\ldots,M_{t,m}^{(\beta,L)} use predictable betting sequences and let nonnegative weights πt,1,…,πt,L\pi_{t,1},\ldots,\pi_{t,L} be ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable with ∑ℓ=1Lπt,ℓ=1\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\pi_{t,\ell}=1. Then Mt,m(β,mix)=∑ℓ=1Lπt,ℓ​Mt,m(β,ℓ)M_{t,m}^{(\beta,\mathrm{mix})}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\pi_{t,\ell}M_{t,m}^{(\beta,\ell)} is a nonnegative supermartingale under the corrected null, and Mt,τt(β,mix)M_{t,\tau_{t}}^{(\beta,\mathrm{mix})} is a conditionally valid e-value at every bounded stopping time.

Proof of Corollary 1.

For each ℓ\ell, conditional supermartingale validity gives

𝔼⁡[Mt,i(β,ℓ)∣ℋt,i−1]≤Mt,i−1(β,ℓ).\mathbb{E}[M_{t,i}^{(\beta,\ell)}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}]\leq M_{t,i-1}^{(\beta,\ell)}.

The weights are nonnegative, sum to one, and are known at ℋt,0=ℱtpre\mathcal{H}_{t,0}=\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}. Hence

𝔼⁡[Mt,i(β,mix)∣ℋt,i−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[M_{t,i}^{(\beta,\mathrm{mix})}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}] =∑ℓ=1Lπt,ℓ​𝔼​[Mt,i(β,ℓ)∣ℋt,i−1]\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\pi_{t,\ell}\mathbb{E}[M_{t,i}^{(\beta,\ell)}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}]
≤∑ℓ=1Lπt,ℓ​Mt,i−1(β,ℓ)=Mt,i−1(β,mix).\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\pi_{t,\ell}M_{t,i-1}^{(\beta,\ell)}=M_{t,i-1}^{(\beta,\mathrm{mix})}.

Nonnegativity is immediate, and bounded optional stopping gives the stopped e-value claim. ∎

𝔼⁡[LT+]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[L_{T}^{+}] =∑t=1T𝔼⁡[It​ℙ​(At=0∣ℱtpre)]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[I_{t}\mathbb{P}(A_{t}=0\mid\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t})\right]
≤e−κ​n​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[It]\displaystyle\leq e^{-\kappa n}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[I_{t}]
≤T​e−κ​n.\displaystyle\leq Te^{-\kappa n}.

The following identity holds on every trajectory:

1−STUT∨1=𝟏{UT=0}+UT−STUT∨1.1-\frac{S_{T}}{U_{T}\vee 1}=\mathbf{1}\{U_{T}=0\}+\frac{U_{T}-S_{T}}{U_{T}\vee 1}.

Indeed, when UT=0U_{T}=0, also ST=0S_{T}=0, and both sides equal one. When UT>0U_{T}>0, the indicator vanishes and the equality follows from UT∨1=UTU_{T}\vee 1=U_{T}. Taking expectations, using UT∨1≥1U_{T}\vee 1\geq 1, and then applying Assumption 2(a), we obtain

1−TER⁡(T)\displaystyle 1-\operatorname{TER}(T) =ℙ⁡(UT=0)+𝔼⁡[LT+UT∨1]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(U_{T}=0)+\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{L_{T}^{+}}{U_{T}\vee 1}\right]
≤ℙ⁡(UT=0)+𝔼⁡[LT+]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}(U_{T}=0)+\mathbb{E}[L_{T}^{+}]
≤rN,n+T​e−κ​n.\displaystyle\leq r_{N,n}+Te^{-\kappa n}.

Rearranging proves Equation (15). Because TT is fixed, rN,n→0r_{N,n}\to 0, and n→∞n\to\infty, the right-hand side tends to zero. Since 0≤TER⁡(T)≤10\leq\operatorname{TER}(T)\leq 1, we conclude that TER⁡(T)→1\operatorname{TER}(T)\to 1. No independence between the future candidate count UTU_{T} and current acceptance decisions is used. ∎

D.2 An explicit conditional miss bound

The following lemma provides the conditional miss bound used to derive Equation (23) in Step 4 of the proof of Theorem 3. Since ηt,i<1\eta_{t,i}<1, every factor in Equation (10) is at least 1−ηt,i>01-\eta_{t,i}>0, so Mt,i(β)>0M^{(\beta)}_{t,i}>0 and its log increments are well defined. For each round with αt>0\alpha_{t}>0, define

Vt,i=log⁡Mt,i(β)Mt,i−1(β),V_{t,i}=\log\frac{M^{(\beta)}_{t,i}}{M^{(\beta)}_{t,i-1}},

and let Lt,iL_{t,i} be the ℋt,i−1\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}-measurable indicator that validation draw ii is made.

Lemma 3 (Conditional miss bound).

Suppose there exist finite ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable gt,ht>0g_{t},h_{t}>0 and finite ℋt,i−1\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}-measurable interval endpoints at,i,bt,ia_{t,i},b_{t,i} such that, on {Δt>0,Lt,i=1}\{\Delta_{t}>0,\ L_{t,i}=1\}, for every i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n,

𝔼⁡[Vt,i∣ℋt,i−1]≥gt,at,i≤Vt,i≤bt,i,bt,i−at,i≤ht.\mathbb{E}[V_{t,i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}]\geq g_{t},\qquad a_{t,i}\leq V_{t,i}\leq b_{t,i},\qquad b_{t,i}-a_{t,i}\leq h_{t}. (26)

Then

ℙ(At=0∣ℱtpre)≤ϵton {Δt>0},\mathbb{P}(A_{t}=0\mid\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t})\leq\epsilon_{t}\qquad\text{on }\{\Delta_{t}>0\},

where

ϵt={exp⁡[−2​nht2​(gt−log⁡(1/αt)n)+2],αt>0,1,αt=0.\epsilon_{t}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\exp\left[-\frac{2n}{h_{t}^{2}}\left(g_{t}-\frac{\log(1/\alpha_{t})}{n}\right)_{+}^{2}\right],&\alpha_{t}>0,\\ 1,&\alpha_{t}=0.\end{cases} (27)
Proof.

If αt=0\alpha_{t}=0, then At=0A_{t}=0 and ϵt=1\epsilon_{t}=1, so the miss bound holds.

Work on the ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable event {Δt>0,αt>0}\{\Delta_{t}>0,\ \alpha_{t}>0\} throughout the following calculation. Define

μt,i=𝔼⁡[Vt,i∣ℋt,i−1],Zt,i=Vt,i−μt,i.\mu_{t,i}=\mathbb{E}[V_{t,i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}],\qquad Z_{t,i}=V_{t,i}-\mu_{t,i}.

On {Lt,i=1}\{L_{t,i}=1\}, Equation (26) gives μt,i≥gt\mu_{t,i}\geq g_{t}, and subtracting μt,i\mu_{t,i} from the interval endpoints preserves their width, which is at most hth_{t}. On {Lt,i=0}\{L_{t,i}=0\}, the evidence is unchanged, so Vt,i=0V_{t,i}=0. Since this event is ℋt,i−1\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}-measurable, μt,i=Zt,i=0\mu_{t,i}=Z_{t,i}=0 there as well. The log increments satisfy Vt,i≤log⁡(1/pε)V_{t,i}\leq\log(1/p_{\varepsilon}) and have nonnegative conditional means on the event under consideration, so their negative parts have conditional expectations at most log⁡(1/pε)\log(1/p_{\varepsilon}). They are therefore integrable when restricted to this event, and 𝔼⁡[Zt,i∣ℋt,i−1]=0\mathbb{E}[Z_{t,i}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}]=0 there.

For any finite nonnegative ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable λ\lambda, the conditional Hoeffding lemma gives

𝔼⁡[e−λ​Zt,i∣ℋt,i−1]≤exp⁡(λ2​ht2/8).\mathbb{E}[e^{-\lambda Z_{t,i}}\mid\mathcal{H}_{t,i-1}]\leq\exp(\lambda^{2}h_{t}^{2}/8).

Both λ\lambda and hth_{t} are fixed when conditioning on ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}. Dividing each factor by exp⁡(λ2​ht2/8)\exp(\lambda^{2}h_{t}^{2}/8) and iterating conditional expectations from ℋt,0=ℱtpre\mathcal{H}_{t,0}=\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t} yields

𝔼[exp{−λ∑i=1nZt,i−n​λ2​ht28}|ℱtpre]≤1.\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left\{-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{t,i}-\frac{n\lambda^{2}h_{t}^{2}}{8}\right\}\middle|\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}\right]\leq 1.

If At=0A_{t}=0, all nn validation draws are made and the evidence never reaches 1/αt1/\alpha_{t}. Therefore,

∑i=1nVt,i=log⁡Mt,n(β)<log⁡(1/αt).\sum_{i=1}^{n}V_{t,i}=\log M^{(\beta)}_{t,n}<\log(1/\alpha_{t}).

On this miss event, Lt,i=1L_{t,i}=1 for every i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. Equation (26) then gives μt,i≥gt\mu_{t,i}\geq g_{t} at every draw, so

∑i=1nμt,i≥n​gt.\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{t,i}\geq ng_{t}.

exp{−λ∑i=1nZt,i−n​λ2​ht28}>exp(λndt−n​λ2​ht28).\exp\left\{-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{t,i}-\frac{n\lambda^{2}h_{t}^{2}}{8}\right\}>\exp\left(\lambda nd_{t}-\frac{n\lambda^{2}h_{t}^{2}}{8}\right).

ℙ⁡(At=0∣ℱtpre)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(A_{t}=0\mid\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}) ≤𝔼[exp{−λ∑i=1nZt,i−n​λ2​ht28}|ℱpret]exp⁡(λ​n​dt−n​λ2​ht28)\displaystyle\leq\frac{\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left\{-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{t,i}-\frac{n\lambda^{2}h_{t}^{2}}{8}\right\}\middle|\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}\right]}{\exp\left(\lambda nd_{t}-\frac{n\lambda^{2}h_{t}^{2}}{8}\right)}
≤1exp⁡(λ​n​dt−n​λ2​ht28)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\exp\left(\lambda nd_{t}-\frac{n\lambda^{2}h_{t}^{2}}{8}\right)}
=exp⁡(−λ​n​dt+n​λ2​ht28).\displaystyle=\exp\left(-\lambda nd_{t}+\frac{n\lambda^{2}h_{t}^{2}}{8}\right).

The second inequality uses the conditional expectation bound of one established above by iterating the conditional Hoeffding bound. D.3 Extension of the power bound to mixtures

Consider the convex mixture in Corollary 1,

Mt,m(β,mix)=∑ℓ=1Lπt,ℓ​Mt,m(β,ℓ),πt,ℓ≥0,∑ℓ=1Lπt,ℓ=1,M_{t,m}^{(\beta,\mathrm{mix})}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\pi_{t,\ell}M_{t,m}^{(\beta,\ell)},\qquad\pi_{t,\ell}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\pi_{t,\ell}=1,

where the weights are ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable and remain fixed during validation. Suppose at least one component ℓ⋆\ell^{\star} has predictable fractions satisfying Assumption 2(c) on draws and weights πt,ℓ⋆≥π∗>0\pi_{t,\ell^{\star}}\geq\pi_{*}>0 for every round and run, with π∗\pi_{*} independent of (N,n)(N,n). Other components need not satisfy this power condition, but they remain nonnegative processes constructed by Equation (10) with predictable fractions in [0,1)[0,1).

Proof.

Nonnegativity gives Mt,m(β,mix)≥π∗​Mt,m(β,ℓ⋆)M_{t,m}^{(\beta,\mathrm{mix})}\geq\pi_{*}M_{t,m}^{(\beta,\ell^{\star})}. If the mixture gate misses an improving candidate, all nn draws are made and

Mt,n(β,mix)<1/αt,Mt,n(β,ℓ⋆)<1/(π∗​αt).M_{t,n}^{(\beta,\mathrm{mix})}<1/\alpha_{t},\qquad M_{t,n}^{(\beta,\ell^{\star})}<1/(\pi_{*}\alpha_{t}).

Steps 2–3 of the proof of Theorem 3 apply to the selected component, with its increments held at zero after the mixture gate stops. The conditional concentration argument in Appendix D.2 therefore gives

ℙ⁡(At=0∣ℱtpre)≤exp⁡[−2​nh2​(gN,n−log⁡(1/(π∗​αt))n)+2]\mathbb{P}(A_{t}=0\mid\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t})\leq\exp\left[-\frac{2n}{h^{2}}\left(g_{N,n}-\frac{\log(1/(\pi_{*}\alpha_{t}))}{n}\right)_{+}^{2}\right]

on {Δt>0}\{\Delta_{t}>0\}. The additional threshold penalty is at most the fixed constant log⁡(1/π∗)\log(1/\pi_{*}). Replacing Λ\Lambda by Λ+log⁡(1/π∗)\Lambda+\log(1/\pi_{*}) in Step 4 thus gives the same e−κ​ne^{-\kappa n} bound for all sufficiently large runs. Step 5 then proves the same TER conclusion. Under Assumption 1, the mixture remains conditionally valid by Corollary 1, so the proof of Theorem 4 below also applies. Only the designated component is required to satisfy the power condition. ∎

Appendix E Proof of the Gain Bound

Define the cumulative loss from accepted updates by

DT−=∑t=1TAt​(−Δt)+.D_{T}^{-}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}A_{t}(-\Delta_{t})_{+}.
Proof of Theorem 4.

Fix a finite horizon T≥1T\geq 1 and the resource sequence and algorithm configuration in Appendix D.1. Take κ>0\kappa>0 as in Equation (24) and consider a sufficiently large run for Equation (25) to hold. Throughout, the candidates, effects, and acceptance decisions refer to the actual adaptive trajectory.

Step 1: Bound cumulative accepted loss.

Under Assumption 1, Theorem 1 and Proposition 1 provide conditionally valid evidence at the gate’s stopping time. Lemma 2 therefore gives

𝔼⁡[Ntε​At∣ℱtpre]≤Ntε​αt.\mathbb{E}[N_{t}^{\varepsilon}A_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}]\leq N_{t}^{\varepsilon}\alpha_{t}.

Let Wt=(−Δt−ε)+W_{t}=(-\Delta_{t}-\varepsilon)_{+}. Since Δt\Delta_{t} is ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable and lies in [−1,1][-1,1], WtW_{t} is bounded, nonnegative, and ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable. Moreover, Wt>0W_{t}>0 implies Δt<−ε\Delta_{t}<-\varepsilon, so Wt=Ntε​WtW_{t}=N_{t}^{\varepsilon}W_{t}. Thus

𝔼⁡[At​Wt]=𝔼⁡[Wt​𝔼​[Ntε​At∣ℱtpre]]≤𝔼⁡[αt​Wt].\mathbb{E}[A_{t}W_{t}]=\mathbb{E}\left[W_{t}\mathbb{E}[N_{t}^{\varepsilon}A_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}]\right]\leq\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{t}W_{t}].

The identity

(−Δt)+=min⁡{(−Δt)+,ε}+(−Δt−ε)+(-\Delta_{t})_{+}=\min\{(-\Delta_{t})_{+},\varepsilon\}+(-\Delta_{t}-\varepsilon)_{+}

splits each accepted loss into the part up to ε\varepsilon and the excess. Multiplying by AtA_{t}, summing, and taking expectations gives

𝔼⁡[DT−]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[D_{T}^{-}] =∑t=1T𝔼⁡[At​min⁡{(−Δt)+,ε}]+∑t=1T𝔼⁡[At​Wt]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[A_{t}\min\{(-\Delta_{t})_{+},\varepsilon\}]+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[A_{t}W_{t}]
≤∑t=1T𝔼⁡[At​min⁡{(−Δt)+,ε}]+∑t=1T𝔼⁡[αt​(−Δt−ε)+].\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[A_{t}\min\{(-\Delta_{t})_{+},\varepsilon\}]+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{t}(-\Delta_{t}-\varepsilon)_{+}].

Step 2: Control MDD.

For every 0≤r<s≤T0\leq r<s\leq T, the update rule implies

J(Θr)−J(Θs)=−∑t=r+1sAtΔt≤∑t=r+1sAt(−Δt)+≤DT−.J(\Theta_{r})-J(\Theta_{s})=-\sum_{t=r+1}^{s}A_{t}\Delta_{t}\leq\sum_{t=r+1}^{s}A_{t}(-\Delta_{t})_{+}\leq D_{T}^{-}.

Taking a positive part and then maximizing over (r,s)(r,s) yields MDD⁡(T)≤DT−\operatorname{MDD}(T)\leq D_{T}^{-} pathwise. Taking expectations and applying Step 1 gives the auxiliary bound

𝔼⁡[MDD⁡(T)]≤∑t=1T𝔼⁡[At​min⁡{(−Δt)+,ε}+αt​(−Δt−ε)+].\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{MDD}(T)]\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[A_{t}\min\{(-\Delta_{t})_{+},\varepsilon\}+\alpha_{t}(-\Delta_{t}-\varepsilon)_{+}\right].

This bound uses only conditional validity, not the power or candidate discovery conditions.

The update rule gives J⁡(Θt)−J⁡(Θt−1)=At​ΔtJ(\Theta_{t})-J(\Theta_{t-1})=A_{t}\Delta_{t}, and At​Δt=It​At​Δt−At​(−Δt)+A_{t}\Delta_{t}=I_{t}A_{t}\Delta_{t}-A_{t}(-\Delta_{t})_{+}. Summing over rounds yields

J⁡(ΘT)−J⁡(Θ0)=∑t=1TAt​Δt=∑t=1TIt​At​Δt−DT−.J(\Theta_{T})-J(\Theta_{0})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}A_{t}\Delta_{t}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}I_{t}A_{t}\Delta_{t}-D_{T}^{-}.

Since It​Δt=(Δt)+I_{t}\Delta_{t}=(\Delta_{t})_{+} is nonnegative and ℱtpre\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}-measurable, the derived conditional miss bound in Equation (25) gives

𝔼⁡[It​At​Δt]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[I_{t}A_{t}\Delta_{t}] =𝔼⁡[(Δt)+​𝔼​[At∣ℱtpre]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[(\Delta_{t})_{+}\mathbb{E}[A_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t}]\right]
≥(1−e−κ​n)​𝔼​[(Δt)+].\displaystyle\geq(1-e^{-\kappa n})\mathbb{E}[(\Delta_{t})_{+}].

Consequently,

G⁡(T)\displaystyle G(T) =∑t=1T𝔼⁡[It​At​Δt]−𝔼⁡[DT−]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[I_{t}A_{t}\Delta_{t}]-\mathbb{E}[D_{T}^{-}]
≥(1−e−κ​n)​𝒫T−∑t=1T𝔼⁡[At​min⁡{(−Δt)+,ε}+αt​(−Δt−ε)+].\displaystyle\geq(1-e^{-\kappa n})\mathcal{P}_{T}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[A_{t}\min\{(-\Delta_{t})_{+},\varepsilon\}+\alpha_{t}(-\Delta_{t}-\varepsilon)_{+}\right].

The last inequality uses Step 1. This proves Equation (16) with the same κ\kappa as in the proof of Theorem 3.

Finally, the same conditional miss bound gives

0≤∑t=1T𝔼⁡[(1−At)​(Δt)+]\displaystyle 0\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[(1-A_{t})(\Delta_{t})_{+}] =∑t=1T𝔼⁡[(Δt)+​ℙ​(At=0∣ℱtpre)]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[(\Delta_{t})_{+}\mathbb{P}(A_{t}=0\mid\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t})\right]
≤e−κ​n​𝒫T\displaystyle\leq e^{-\kappa n}\mathcal{P}_{T}
≤T​e−κ​n⟶0,\displaystyle\leq Te^{-\kappa n}\longrightarrow 0,

since 𝒫T≤T\mathcal{P}_{T}\leq T and TT is fixed. This establishes the vanishing missed-improvement claim accompanying the theorem. The accepted-loss terms need not vanish. Neither the loss bound nor the weighted miss calculation requires independence across rounds or comparison to a different candidate trajectory. ∎

Appendix F Harness Design with Four Components and Operators

This appendix describes the operators used in our experiments. Operator names remain fixed across benchmarks. The specific details of the operators are adapted to suit different benchmarks.

F.1 State representation

Inspired by modular agent design and automated agent search in AgentSquare and ADAS (Shang et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025), we organize the mutable agent state into four editable components: reasoning, routing, memory, and workflow. The four-component representation and the specific operator definitions below are implementation choices of our harness.

The mutable harness state is

𝖧=(𝖱,𝖯,𝖬,𝖶),\mathsf{H}=(\mathsf{R},\mathsf{P},\mathsf{M},\mathsf{W}),

where 𝖱\mathsf{R} is the reasoning strategy, 𝖯\mathsf{P} is the context router/provider, 𝖬\mathsf{M} is episodic memory, and 𝖶\mathsf{W} is workflow. These components determine the instructions and context for a single solver call.

A proposed transition has the structured form

ot=(κt,operator,target,parameters),o_{t}=(\kappa_{t},\texttt{operator},\texttt{target},\texttt{parameters}),

where κt∈{𝖱,𝖯,𝖬,𝖶}\kappa_{t}\in\{\mathsf{R},\mathsf{P},\mathsf{M},\mathsf{W}\} identifies the component to modify; operator specifies the operation to perform; target identifies the rule, memory entry, or configuration field to which the operation applies; and parameters supplies the values or content required by that operation. For example, refining an existing reasoning rule uses κt=𝖱\kappa_{t}=\mathsf{R}, operator=REFINE_RULE, the rule identifier as target, and the revised procedure in parameters.

F.2 Reasoning operators

Motivated by prior work on modular reasoning, decomposition, self-refinement, and prompt scope (Zhou et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023; Fernando et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024), we represent the reasoning strategy as an explicit and editable rule set. The corresponding operators allow reasoning rules and decomposition policies to be added, revised, generalized, reprioritized, or removed based on closed historical feedback. The particular typed rule schema and operator definitions are implementation choices of our harness.

The reasoning component stores the base analysis protocol, decomposition policy, and a bounded collection of specialist rules. It is compiled into the mutable analysis instruction of the existing solver and does not alter the fixed role prompt.

F.3 Routing operators

Motivated by retrieval-augmented generation, adaptive retrieval, evolving retrieval policies, and selective context construction (Lewis et al., 2020; Asai et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2023), we treat routing as an editable pre-solver information-access policy. Its operators control how available context is selected, ranked, expanded, truncated, or restored before the solver call.

The routing component controls how the existing Wikipedia provider selects and orders passages before the single solver call. It cannot write memory, inspect labels from the current unfinished round, or trigger an additional model call.

F.4 Memory operators

Drawing on episodic reflection, experiential learning, reusable procedural memory, and adaptive memory retrieval (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026), we treat memory as a persistent editable experience bank whose entries can be added, revised, selectively triggered and prioritized, or removed across evolution rounds.

The memory component maintains a retrievable active bank. The current protocol does not expose exact or global as proposer-selectable episodic triggers: new episodic memories enter a common cluster-ranking path.

F.5 Workflow operators

Drawing on automated and evolutionary workflow optimization (Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2026), we treat the within-call execution workflow as an editable state that can evolve across rounds through changes to verification, evidence alignment, stopping, and fallback policies.

The workflow component specifies a plan →\rightarrow reason →\rightarrow check →\rightarrow finalize policy within the same completion. It does not add a second verifier or a hidden model call.

Appendix G Experiment Details

G.1 Common protocol

We evaluate Greedy, PACE, SGM-B, SGM-H, and TRUST on HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with Qwen-3.8-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Each method runs for 30 outer rounds. For HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS, solver output seeds range from 0 to 4 and data split seeds range from 42 to 46. Within each setting, all methods share the same initial test responses. Throughout the experiments, we reuse cached responses for identical inputs whenever possible to ensure fair comparisons across methods. One candidate is then selected for validation on up to 40 examples sampled without replacement from the 200-example validation pool; validation samples may overlap across rounds. The initial set contains 20 examples and the validation pool contains 200 examples. All four components and 20 operators in Appendix F are available. Performance is evaluated on 300 held-out test examples, which are used only for reporting.

In each setting, all gates start from the same initial harness, which contains prespecified weaknesses that provide clear opportunities for improvement. This design allows us to examine whether different gates accept candidates that correct these weaknesses. In later rounds, when the incumbent has typically reached a higher level of performance, we also examine whether the gates reject subsequent candidates that could reduce performance and cause the agent to lose earlier gains. The experiments therefore examine different stages of the RSI process, from repairing initial weaknesses to preserving improvements during continued search.

For API calls, we configure the generation parameters as follows. All roles use top-p = 1. The temperature is set to 0 for the Solver and Allocator, and to 0.3 for the Proposer, except for HotpotQA with DeepSeek, where the Proposer uses 0.7. The Solver’s maximum output length is 512, 768, and 8192 tokens for HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS, respectively, while the Allocator uses a uniform limit of 4096 tokens. The Proposer’s maximum output length is 2400 tokens, except on HotpotQA, where DeepSeek and Qwen use limits of 1536 and 2048 tokens, respectively.

We use an equally weighted mixture of four betting strategies, with (ηt,i(1),ηt,i(2),ηt,i(3),ηt,i(4))=(0.10,0.25,0.50,0.75)(\eta_{t,i}^{(1)},\eta_{t,i}^{(2)},\eta_{t,i}^{(3)},\eta_{t,i}^{(4)})=(0.10,0.25,0.50,0.75) for all t,it,i and mixture weights πt,ℓ=1/4\pi_{t,\ell}=1/4 for ℓ=1,…,4\ell=1,\ldots,4. The resulting statistic is Mt,m(β,mix)=14​∑ℓ=14Mt,m(β,ℓ)M_{t,m}^{(\beta,\mathrm{mix})}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\ell=1}^{4}M_{t,m}^{(\beta,\ell)}.

G.2 Metrics

For each seed b∈{1,…,B}b\in\{1,\ldots,B\}, let J^b,t\widehat{J}_{b,t} denote the mean task score of the incumbent after round tt on NtestN_{\mathrm{test}} held-out test examples, measured on the [0,1][0,1] scale. Test results are used only for reporting. Let J^b,tcand\widehat{J}^{\mathrm{cand}}_{b,t} denote the corresponding score of the selected candidate, and define

Δ^b,t=J^b,tcand−J^b,t−1.\widehat{\Delta}_{b,t}=\widehat{J}^{\mathrm{cand}}_{b,t}-\widehat{J}_{b,t-1}.

Let 𝒞b\mathcal{C}_{b} denote the rounds with an available selected candidate up to round TT, and let Ab,tA_{b,t} indicate acceptance. We first compute each metric within each seed and then average across seeds:

G^Ntest​(T)\displaystyle\widehat{G}_{N_{\mathrm{test}}}(T) =1B​∑b=1B(J^b,T−J^b,0),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\bigl(\widehat{J}_{b,T}-\widehat{J}_{b,0}\bigr), MDD^Ntest​(T)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathrm{MDD}}_{N_{\mathrm{test}}}(T) =1B​∑b=1Bmax0≤r<s≤T⁡(J^b,r−J^b,s)+,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\max_{0\leq r<s\leq T}\bigl(\widehat{J}_{b,r}-\widehat{J}_{b,s}\bigr)_{+},
FER^0,Ntest​(T)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathrm{FER}}_{0,N_{\mathrm{test}}}(T) =1B​∑b=1B∑t∈𝒞bAb,t𝟏{Δ^b,t≤0}(∑t∈𝒞bAb,t)∨1,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}_{b}}A_{b,t}\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{\Delta}_{b,t}\leq 0\}}{\left(\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}_{b}}A_{b,t}\right)\vee 1}, TER^Ntest​(T)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathrm{TER}}_{N_{\mathrm{test}}}(T) =1B​∑b=1B∑t∈𝒞bAb,t𝟏{Δ^b,t>0}(∑t∈𝒞b𝟏{Δ^b,t>0})∨1.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}_{b}}A_{b,t}\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{\Delta}_{b,t}>0\}}{\left(\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}_{b}}\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{\Delta}_{b,t}>0\}\right)\vee 1}.

We use Ntest=300N_{\mathrm{test}}=300, T=30T=30, and B=5B=5. Gain and MDD are reported in percentage points (pp), while FER0 and TER are reported as percentages. FER0 counts accepted non-improving updates, including ties. The TER denominator counts improving selected candidates, including those rejected by the gate. A run with no accepted updates contributes zero to both FER0 and TER.

G.3 Proposer and Solver

The proposer generates three proposals using feedback from completed rounds. We screen the candidates on 20 examples from the previous round and select the valid candidate with the highest score for the current round. To minimize the effect of unequal feedback sample sizes on the proposer, we retain all 40 examples for feedback even when TRUST’s statistical test stops early. Exposure probabilities in subsequent rounds therefore account for the full batch rather than only the observations up to the stopping time.

Here, we present example designs for the Proposer and Solver on HotpotQA. The proposer template guides candidate generation using the current harness and previously closed feedback. And the solver template guides task execution using the current harness policies and a fixed output contract.

G.4 Case study for Greedy

We follow the experimental protocol in Appendix G.1. In APPS, the solver writes a program from a problem description, and the program is evaluated using test cases. We examine a workflow update accepted by Greedy in the main experiment with DeepSeek-V4-Flash and seed 0. This case illustrates how Greedy can be misled by sampling noise in a finite validation set, accepting an update that improves validation performance while reducing performance on held-out test problems.

In round 17, the incumbent uses the following workflow.

⬇
{
"verify_mode": "light",
"evidence_alignment": "spec_and_examples",
"stop_rule": "first_parseable_program",
"fallback_mode": "best_effort"
}

The proposer suggests changing the stop_rule field to address cases where the solver returns no code or generates a program that produces incorrect answers.

⬇
{
"component": "workflow",
"operator": "SET_STOP_RULE",
"parameters": {
"stop_rule": "first_example_pass"
},
"observed_failure": "Closed failures include 21 schema_failure cases with no_code and 27 wrong_answer cases; many generated programs fail on supplied tests, indicating the solver may not validate against examples before finalizing.",
"expected_local_benefit": "Switching the stop rule to first_example_pass will require the solver to verify its program against the first supplied example before stopping, catching obvious I/O mismatches and reducing wrong_answer and schema_failure cases.",
"possible_regression": "May cause the solver to stop prematurely if the first example is not representative, but the change is minimal and reversible."
}

The proposer changes the incumbent’s stop_rule to first_example_pass, asking the solver to consider whether its program would pass the first supplied example before finishing. It changes the one call workflow instruction and the other workflow fields remain unchanged.

We first examine an Emotional Sort problem from the sampled validation set.

⬇
You’ll have a function called "**sortEmotions**" that will return an array of **emotions** sorted. It has two parameters, the first parameter called "**arr**" will expect an array of **emotions** where an **emotion** will be one of the following:
- **:D** -> Super Happy
- **:)** -> Happy
- **:|** -> Normal
- **:(** -> Sad
- **T\_T** -> Super Sad
Example of the array:‘‘[ ’T_T’, ’:D’, ’:|’, ’:)’, ’:(’ ]‘‘
And the second parameter is called "**order**", if this parameter is **true** then the order of the emotions will be descending (from **Super Happy** to **Super Sad**) if it’s **false** then it will be ascending (from **Super Sad** to **Super Happy**)
Example if **order** is true with the above array: ‘‘[ ’:D’, ’:)’, ’:|’, ’:(’, ’T_T’ ]‘‘
- Super Happy -> Happy -> Normal -> Sad -> Super Sad
If **order** is false: ‘‘[ ’T_T’, ’:(’, ’:|’, ’:)’, ’:D’ ]‘‘
- Super Sad -> Sad -> Normal -> Happy -> Super Happy
Example:
‘‘‘
arr = [’:D’, ’:|’, ’:)’, ’:(’, ’:D’]
sortEmotions(arr, true) // [ ’:D’, ’:D’, ’:)’, ’:|’, ’:(’ ]
sortEmotions(arr, false) // [ ’:(’, ’:|’, ’:)’, ’:D’, ’:D’ ]
‘‘‘

The Emotional Sort problem asks the solver to write a function that sorts a list of emotion symbols by their happiness levels. The symbols have a fixed order from happiest to saddest: :D, :), :|, :(, and T_T. The parameter order determines the sorting direction: true requires the happiest emotions first, while false requires the saddest emotions first.

⬇
def sort_emotions(arr, order):
# Define the order of emotions from Super Happy to Super Sad
emotion_order = [’:D’, ’:)’, ’:|’, ’:(’, ’T_T’]
# Create a mapping from emotion to its rank
rank = {emotion: i for i, emotion in enumerate(emotion_order)}
# Sort the array based on the rank
# If order is True, sort descending (Super Happy first)
# If order is False, sort ascending (Super Sad first)
sorted_arr = sorted(arr, key=lambda x: rank[x], reverse=order)
return sorted_arr

The incumbent assigns rank 00 to the happiest emotion and rank 44 to the saddest, but uses reverse=order. When order=True, this places the saddest emotions first, contrary to the task requirement. The candidate corrects the sorting direction: it sorts by increasing rank when order=True and by decreasing rank when order=False. The incumbent response incorrectly treats order=True, which requests the happiest emotions first, as reverse=True, which places the largest rank first and therefore puts the saddest emotions first.

⬇
def sort_emotions(arr, order):
# Define the order of emotions from Super Happy to Super Sad
emotion_order = [’:D’, ’:)’, ’:|’, ’:(’, ’T_T’]
# If order is true, sort descending (Super Happy first)
# If order is false, sort ascending (Super Sad first)
# Use the index in emotion_order as the sort key
# For descending, sort by negative index; for ascending, sort by index
if order:
return sorted(arr, key=lambda e: emotion_order.index(e))
else:
return sorted(arr, key=lambda e: emotion_order.index(e), reverse=True)

The candidate corrects the branch logic. It sorts by increasing index when order is true and reverses the order when it is false, matching the problem’s specification.

⬇
{
"accepted": true,
"outer_effect_geometry": {

"candidate_wins": 4,
"incumbent_wins": 2,
"ties": 34,

},

Four problem scores improve, two decline, and 34 stay unchanged. Besides Emotional Sort, two graph problems improve from invalid responses to 4/5. These gains are accompanied by two complete regressions. The mean score rises from 60.50% to 64.50% on the validation set, so Greedy accepts the candidate.

We next examine a test problem about the number of days off in a Martian year.

⬇
On the planet Mars a year lasts exactly n days (there are no leap years on Mars). But Martians have the same weeks as earthlings— 5 work days and then 2 days off. Your task is to determine the minimum possible and the maximum possible number of days off per year on Mars.
-----Input-----
The first line of the input contains a positive integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 1 000 000) — the number of days in a year on Mars.
-----Output-----
Print two integers — the minimum possible and the maximum possible number of days off per year on Mars.
-----Examples-----
Input
14
Output
4 4
Input
2
Output
0 2

A full seven-day week contains two days off. For n=7​w+rn=7w+r, with 0≤r<70\leq r<7, the required minimum and maximum are 2​w+max⁡(0,r−5)2w+\max(0,r-5) and 2​w+min⁡(r,2)2w+\min(r,2). The first example has no remainder, while the second directly tests a partial week.

The number of days off depends on which day of the week the year begins. Every complete seven-day period contains exactly two days off, while any remaining days may include additional days off. For n=14n=14, the year contains exactly two full weeks, so both the minimum and maximum are four. For n=2n=2, the two days could both be workdays or both be days off, giving a minimum of zero and a maximum of two. The incumbent and candidate receive the same complete problem statement, including both examples.

⬇
def main():
data = sys.stdin.read().strip().split()
if not data:
return
n = int(data[0])
full_weeks = n // 7
rem = n % 7
min_off = full_weeks * 2
max_off = full_weeks * 2
min_off = full_weeks * 2 + max(0, rem - 5)
max_off = full_weeks * 2 + min(rem, 2)
print(min_off, max_off)
if __name__ == "__main__":
main()

The incumbent counts two days off for each full week and then accounts for the remaining days. In particular, min(rem, 2) adds the maximum possible number of days off among those remaining days. This program passes all five evaluation test cases.

⬇
def main():
data = sys.stdin.read().strip().split()
if not data:
return
n = int(data[0])
full_weeks = n // 7
rem = n % 7
min_off = full_weeks * 2
max_off = full_weeks * 2
min_off += max(0, rem - 5)
print(min_off, max_off)
if __name__ == "__main__":
main()

The candidate correctly computes the minimum number of days off, but counts only complete weeks when computing the maximum, ignoring possible days off in the remaining days. For the first example, n=14n=14, there are no remaining days, so the candidate still returns the correct output, 4 4. For the second example, n=2n=2, there are no full weeks, so it incorrectly returns 0 0 instead of 0 2. This behavior is consistent with the first_example_pass instruction: the first supplied example does not show this error, while the second does. Finally, the candidate passes only one of the five evaluation test cases, compared with all five for the incumbent.

⬇
{
"metrics": {
"items": 300,
"mean_per_problem_test_pass_fraction": 0.7506666666666666,
"schema_parse_failures": 37,

}
