Across all 300 test problems, the mean fraction of passed test cases falls from 75.07%75.07\% for the incumbent to 67.00%67.00\% for the candidate. Although the update changes only one workflow instruction, it changes the solver’s stopping criterion and may encourage it to focus on matching the first supplied example. In the Martian year problem, the first supplied example contains only complete weeks, so matching it does not require correct handling of the remaining days. The candidate’s missing calculation illustrates how a program can satisfy this narrower requirement while failing other cases. In this case, the update improves validation performance but reduces performance on the held-out test problems.

Appendix H Supplementary Sensitivity Analysis

H.1 Parameter sensitivity analysis

This appendix supplements the sensitivity analysis in Section 6.2. We conduct the experiments on HotpotQA using DeepSeek-V4-Flash. The reported one-parameter grids are q∈{0.1,0.3,0.5}q\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5\}, ε∈{0,0.05,0.1,0.15}\varepsilon\in\{0,0.05,0.1,0.15\}, and β∈{0,0.01,0.03,0.05}\beta\in\{0,0.01,0.03,0.05\}, around (q,ε,β)=(0.30,0.10,0.01)(q,\varepsilon,\beta)=(0.30,0.10,0.01).

Tables 7–9 report the three parameters separately. Each setting is summarized as mean ±\pm standard error (SE).

In Figure 7, the parameters affect how much performance improves and whether that improvement lasts. With q=0.1q=0.1, the mean trajectory first rises at round 9 and reaches a lower final score; q=0.3q=0.3 improves earlier, whereas q=0.5q=0.5 shows a late change in the acceptance decision without a higher final score. For the margin, ε=0\varepsilon=0 produces no accepted updates, and ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05 delays improvement until round 21. Increasing the margin ε\varepsilon to 0.15 yields early gains but subsequent fluctuations. MDD rises from 0.02 pp to 5.33 pp. For the overlap correction strength, β=0\beta=0 shows a late decline, while β=0.01\beta=0.01 retains a similar peak with little subsequent loss. Larger correction strengths of 0.03 and 0.05 reduce gains to 7.13 pp and 2.80 pp.

H.2 LLM allocator analysis

This section provides a case study to supplement the LLM ablation study in Section 6.2. We examine HotpotQA/DeepSeek-V4-Flash with seed 3, comparing TRUST with an ablation that replaces the LLM allocator with a fixed multiplier wt=1w_{t}=1. The proposer, solver and statistical testing are unchanged. Historical information offers identical parent states, candidates, results and evidence before round 2. Both methods reject in round 1, and their acceptance decisions first diverge in round 2.

The following excerpt shows the relevant reasoning fields of the incumbent shared by both paths before round 2.

Select only the first displayed title and ignore all later titles and sentences. Verify: Assume the first title is sufficient evidence without checking its text. Do not verify entity identity or cross-title links. Repair: Skip bridge reasoning and do not combine facts from different paragraphs. Skip comparisons and use the first title regardless of the requested relation. Finalize: Return the first displayed title as the answer and cite sentence 0 from that title.",
"decomposition_policy": "",

}
}

It proposes breaking questions that involve multiple entities into sub-questions. The update leaves the following instruction unchanged: Select only the first displayed title and ignore all later titles and sentences.

The expected scores for the five dimensions of safety, contract, actionability, generalization, and scope control are (2,4,3,2,4)(2,4,3,2,4), respectively. The allocator combines the LLM scores with the very_conservative recommendation to determine the LLM multiplier and testing level. This produces a stricter acceptance threshold than the baseline with wt≡1w_{t}\equiv 1. Given the same validation evidence, TRUST rejects the candidate while the baseline accepts it, leading to different subsequent search trajectories. Although the rejected candidate also improves on the initial incumbent, TRUST later accepts a candidate with a larger gain on the test set. For this seed, TRUST finishes at Joint F1 47.22%, compared with 43.95% for the baseline. This case illustrates how the LLM module can influence allocation and subsequent search through assessments of each candidate and its context. These assessments guide the testing level within the statistical gate, preserving FER control.

Appendix I Overfitting Study

Here, we analyze an overfitting stress test based on our harness design in Appendix F, using Greedy as the acceptance gate. Figure 8 shows the mean gain trajectories of the Greedy gate on HotpotQA Distractor using DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Joint F1 over solver seeds s=0,…,4s=0,\ldots,4 and data-split seeds 42+s42+s. Each run reuses 20 fixed examples for proposing and validation and the test set contains 100 examples. Each round proposes one routing or memory update using closed historical feedback and accepts it only if Joint F1 improves on the fixed validation set. Reasoning and workflow remain frozen.

Mechanism and interpretation.

Routing selects the evidence paragraphs shown to the solver for the current question, while memory provides retrieved cases and feedback from previous tasks. Their interaction involves both a shared context budget and different retrieval modes, which affect which evidence paragraphs are selected and how many are retained. This design is motivated by work on retrieval and context utilization (Shi et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024).

Figure 8 shows that mean validation gain reaches 24.44 pp as the same data are reused for proposing and validation. Relative to round 0, mean test gain peaks at 5.06 pp after round 1, then falls to -2.15 pp by round 10. This divergence suggests that iterative harness optimization can overfit reused proposal and validation data.

I.1 Case study for overfitting

On the HotpotQA benchmark (Yang et al., 2018), a system answers questions that require combining information from multiple Wikipedia articles. It must also identify the supporting facts, namely the specific sentences in the provided paragraphs that together justify the answer. We present a concrete example below.

⬇
What is the name of the lead remix of the track from the remix album containing remixes of the lady gaga studio album "The Fame"?

The correct answer is Bad Romance. The supporting facts establish two connections. First, The Remix contains remixes of songs from Lady Gaga’s studio album The Fame. Second, Starsmith’s remix of Bad Romance was selected as the lead remix on The Remix. Before the update, the incumbent retrieves no case memory and selects eight of the ten available paragraphs, including the required sources.

⬇
{
"final_answer": "Starsmith Remix",
"supporting_facts": [
{"title": "Starsmith", "sentence_id": 4}
],
"atomic_facts": [
{"subject": "Starsmith", "relation": "remixed",
"object": "Bad Romance",
"title": "Starsmith", "sentence_id": 4},
{"subject": "Starsmith’s remix of Bad Romance", "relation": "was chosen as lead remix on",
"object": "The Remix",
"title": "Starsmith", "sentence_id": 4}
],
"reasoning": {"operation": "bridge", "fact_indices": [0, 1],
"result": "Starsmith Remix"}
}

The response identifies the remix relationship but returns Starsmith Remix as the answer. It also omits sentence 1 of The Remix (Lady Gaga album) from its supporting facts. The answer is incorrect, and Joint F1 is 0. The proposer reflects on this failure and proposes adding the following episodic memory.

⬇
{
"memory_id": "mem-f52c9c540a60",
"question_text": "What is the name of the lead remix of the track from the remix album containing remixes of the lady gaga studio album \"The Fame\"?",
"verified_answer": "Bad Romance",
"support_facts": [["Starsmith", 4], ["The Remix (Lady Gaga album)", 1]],

"fame",

"For a non-identical cluster match, treat the episode only as an analogy and verify both bridge hops."
],
"supporting_fact_policy": "Return only supporting facts grounded in the current Wikipedia context."
}

This episode stores the full validation question, its verified answer, and both supporting-fact locations. Its procedure permits answer reuse for an identical question. If a different question retrieves this memory, the solver is instructed to analyze the question using both the retrieved memory and the current Wikipedia context, and to verify that both reasoning steps are supported by evidence in that context. Retrieval compares the words in the current question with those in the stored question.

For the repeated validation question, the system retrieves the stored memory as an exact match and supplies its verified answer and supporting fact locations to the solver. The selected context still includes both required evidence sources.

We now turn to the test set and consider the following example.

⬇
2014 S/S is the debut album of a South Korean boy group that was formed by who?

The correct answer is YG Entertainment. The question asks who formed the South Korean boy group whose debut album is 2014 S/S. Answering it requires connecting two pieces of information. First, the paragraph from 2014 S/S identifies WINNER as the group that released the album. Second, the paragraph from Winner (band) states that WINNER was formed by YG Entertainment. Together, these facts connect the album to the group and then to the organization that formed it. Before the update, the incumbent selects eight of the ten available paragraphs, including both of these sources.

⬇
{
"final_answer": "YG Entertainment",
"supporting_facts": [
{"title": "2014 S/S", "sentence_id": 0},
{"title": "Winner (band)", "sentence_id": 0}

This question retrieves the Lady Gaga memory through the same keyword album. After retrieving this memory, the system changes how it selects evidence paragraphs and limits the number retained in the context. This sentence concerns the album’s release by a record label. It does not establish who formed the group. The answer happens to remain correct, so Answer F1 remains 1, while supporting fact F1 and Joint F1 fall to 0. On the full test set, the accepted update lowers the mean Joint F1 from 54.55% to 48.00%: 13 items decline and none improve. This example shows how a memory can repair a repeated validation question while causing evidence selection to lose a required source on a new question.
